text: Voxie is a dense product that carries a lot of data and complex functionality. The design's job is to make it feel light and approachable. This is achieved through soft shapes, carefully chosen accents, and content that lifts off a quiet page. It should feel like the kind of message the platform sends, friendly and worth reading.

heading: Friendly
text: Surfaces and buttons are heavily rounded. Solid icons also have rounding but more subtly so they stay recognizable at small sizes. Ample white space gives the eye places to rest. Accents use light fill colors with dark text. Motion is quick and gentle, nothing bounces.

heading: Clear
text: White cards group related content over a grey background so information rises up in an organized way. Grids provide the underlying page structure. Headings rely more on weight than size so they stand out even at smaller scales. Every input carries a label so there's never any confusion about what goes in a field. Color is used sparingly to highlight clear calls to action or important data. Color is one of the most attention grabbing elements in a design. If everything has color, then nothing stands out.

Voxie's color palette relies on Tailwind under the hood. The colors are used unchanged but we focus in on a limited subset of colors for most uses. Every color goes by its real name: sky, teal, slate. There are no semantic aliases like primary or danger in the code. A component takes color="sky", not color="primary", so what you read in a class list is what you see on screen. Meaning lives in the guidance below, not in the token name.

heading: Slate
text: Almost everything on screen is slate. It's the page, the panels, the text, and most of the buttons. The other colors are exceptions you reach for deliberately. Slate is a ladder of surfaces, lightest to darkest. The page sits in the middle of the range, so panels can rise above or sink below it: white Card default. The workhorse panel. slate-50 Card glass. Lets inputs stand out from the panel. slate-200 The page background, carried on body. Everything else is measured against this. slate-300/30 Card sunken. Sidebars and collapsible containers. slate-700 Card dark. Only the app navigation bar.

heading: Neutrals step, they don't jump
text: A neutral element sits about one rung away from whatever is behind it. A slate Button reads what it is sitting on from the Card or Navbar wrapping it, and takes sitsOn only where nothing above it can answer. | Behind it | Neutral element | On hover | | ------------ | --------------- | --------- | | white | slate-100 | slate-200 | | slate-50 | slate-200 | slate-300 | | slate-300/30 | slate-300 | slate-400 | | slate-200 | slate-300 | slate-400 | | slate-700 | slate-600 | slate-500 | Hover moves one more rung in the same direction, further from the background. On the dark surface that means moving lighter, since darker would sink the element into the panel.

heading: Accent colors
text: An accent shows up at one of two weights. Which one depends on whether you can press it. Controls, which are anything pressable, rest at 300. Hover is one step darker at 400, and the label is black. Button is the one that matters today. Labels, which are read only, use tints. That is a 100 fill, the 900 of the same hue for the text, a 300 border, and a 500 icon. Badge and Alert both run on it. A control needs to stand out on screen, so it takes the saturated rung. A label repeats and has to sit still while you read past it, so it takes the tint. The tint also measures better at the smaller label sizes. See Contrast for details. Two things hold across both families: One weight per family, for all five accents. No accent appears at any other value in a component. That's what keeps a screen with four colors on it from looking like four different products. Accents don't care what they sit on, unlike slate. A sky button is sky-300 on a white card and on the dark navigation bar. A control at 300 is saturated enough to separate from any neutral behind it. A label at 100 isn't, which is why the tint carries a 300 border rather than a bare fill. Be reserved and tasteful with color. Avoid rainbow screens with tons of colors. This matters most on data-rich screens like tables and charts. Color goes sparingly on the most important details of a page. If everything has a color, nothing is important, and the page looks like a mess. That can't always be avoided, for instance a chart with ten keys that have to be told apart, but try your best. The palette is sky, teal, amber, rose, violet. For the chart with ten keys, Badge carries seven more tints on the label weight: lime, orange, green, blue, fuchsia, pink, and emerald. They exist to extend the range of difference between badges, nothing more. None of them carries a meaning. Outside a legend or a column of tags there's no reason to reach for one.

heading: Text
text: Text sitting on a surface uses four colors, and only four. slate-700 is the default. Body copy on a surface sits at 700, never black or slate-950. Those are for labels on a fill. It has room to spare on every surface: 10.4:1 on white, 9.9:1 on glass, 8.4:1 on the page background, and 7.9:1 on the sunken surface. slate-800 is a step forward, not the default. Headings take it. So does anything that has to cut through a paragraph rather than sit in it: strong, bold, code, and quotes. slate-500 is a step back for supporting copy, not a disabled state. It clears AA on white (4.8:1) and on glass (4.6:1). On the sunken surface it drops to 3.7:1, and on the page background to 3.9:1. On those two, use it only at large sizes, or move the text onto a card. sky-700 marks links. It sits at 700, not the accents' 300, because a link has to be legible as text. It clears AA everywhere, down to 4.5:1 on the sunken surface. sky-600 is the tempting alternative, and it falls short at 4.0:1 on white, under the 4.5:1 AA asks. None of this needs setting by hand. body carries text-slate-700, and prose is pointed at all four, so text inherits the right color on its own. Reach for a utility only to step something back to slate-500. The one surface that flips the rule is the dark card, which sets its own light text.

heading: Labels on a fill
text: A label sitting on a fill is black, not slate-800. A fill is a small, saturated shape holding a couple of words, and it wants the maximum the ramp offers. | Behind the label | Label color | | -------------------------- | ------------------ | | any accent at 300 | black | | white, slate-50 to 300 | black | | slate-600, slate-700 | white | | any accent at its 100 tint | the 900 of the hue | The tint is the one row that isn't black. Black on a 100 fill reads as body copy with a tinted box around it, so the label takes the 900 of the same hue, which also measures better. White on a light fill is never the answer. White on sky-300 lands at 1.67:1. There is one exception. An element with no fill of its own sits directly on the panel, so on the dark surface it takes white. Black on slate-700 would be 2.0:1.

heading: Contrast
text: Every label pairing clears WCAG AAA. The narrowest is white on slate-600 at 7.6:1, against the 7:1 AAA asks of body text. The tables carry two columns, because the two models disagree in ways worth seeing. WCAG 2.x is the ratio every audit and checker reports. APCA is the perceptual model behind the WCAG 3 draft. Its Lc is a score, not a ratio, and it has no pass or fail grade. Roughly, Lc 75 suits body text, Lc 60 larger or heavier text, and Lc 45 headlines. Values below the Lc 75 mark are in rose. Controls, at 300 with a black label: | Fill | Label | WCAG 2.x | APCA | | ---------- | ----- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | sky-300 | black | 12.6:1 | Lc 75 | | teal-300 | black | 14.3:1 | Lc 82 | | amber-300 | black | 14.5:1 | Lc 83 | | rose-300 | black | 10.9:1 | Lc 67 | | violet-300 | black | 11.3:1 | Lc 69 | | slate-100 | black | 19.2:1 | Lc 100 | | slate-300 | black | 14.2:1 | Lc 81 | | slate-600 | white | 7.6:1 | Lc 91 | The three in rose are a known gap, kept for now so the documentation matches what the product ships. They pass every WCAG check, and a contrast tool will call them AAA. WCAG 2.x is generous to dark text on saturated light fills, though. APCA prices sky, rose, and violet below what it wants for text at button size. Buttons run 12–14px, which is where that shortfall counts most. Labels, on the tint: | Fill | Label | WCAG 2.x | APCA | | ---------- | ---------- | -------- | ------ | | sky-100 | sky-900 | 8.2:1 | Lc 82 | | teal-100 | teal-900 | 8.4:1 | Lc 83 | | amber-100 | amber-900 | 8.2:1 | Lc 83 | | rose-100 | rose-900 | 8.0:1 | Lc 78 | | violet-100 | violet-900 | 9.3:1 | Lc 83 | | slate-100 | slate-900 | 16.3:1 | Lc 98 | Nothing here falls short. Lightening the fill is what closes the gap, and it's the label family's answer, not a control's. A 100 fill sits lighter than the page background (rose-100 on slate-200 is 1.02:1), so a control on it couldn't be found before it was read. Controls stay at 300 until there's something better. The soft step between a neutral and its background lands between 1.1:1 and 1.4:1. A slate-100 button on a white card is 1.10:1. That's deliberate, and it's what makes the interface feel calm. It's also below the 3:1 that WCAG asks for the boundary of a control, so the fill alone can't be what tells someone a control is there: The label carries the contrast. Never build a neutral control whose meaning depends on noticing the fill. When a neutral control has to read as a control at a glance, give it shadow or outline for a real edge. Never signal state with a one-rung neutral shift. Nobody will see it.

heading: Charts
text: A categorical chart colors its keys by how many there are, not by what they are. The exception is a chart whose key names match a named set, which colors it instead.

heading: The chart palette
text: Every hue carries three steps, copied from Tailwind. Change what a chart draws by picking a different step, never by editing or interpolating a value. A new hue arrives with all three steps.

heading: Which step gets drawn
text: The mark is the slice, bar, line, or circle. The label background sits behind a legend pill, a chip, or a connecting flow. Both come from one lookup, so a mark and its label are always one hue. The label background is always 300, with a black label like any other label on a fill.

heading: Color by count
text: Each count gets a fixed set, tuned for contrast. Counts clamp to 1 through 12. Zero, or a count that isn't a number, falls to one. Past twelve keys, roll the extras into the last one and label it Other. The twelve-key set ends in slate, so that bucket comes out grey and the eleven keys worth reading keep their hues. Each row is its own set rather than a prefix of the next, and hues get inserted mid-sequence. Teal is sixth of seven and seventh of eight. Sky is the whole one-key set, gone from two through eleven, back at twelve. So a chart that gains a key does not keep its colors. Contrast across the set beats one series holding its color. Where a color has to mean the same thing on every card, use a named set. Two rules hold across the table. Every set is a subsequence of one canonical order, spectral with slate last, so blue always precedes amber and slate is always last. And counts 2 through 12 only add. The one break is 1 to 2, where sky drops out for blue. One key is sky, since a single series has nothing to hold contrast against and sky reads lighter under a card's ink. A single-series chart takes it rather than a hardcoded blue. Two or more keys start at blue. Slate arrives at five, where a set gets a "rest of them" bucket, and is last from there on.

heading: Named sets
text: A named set binds a hue to a meaning, so a suspended group is rose on every card that draws one rather than rose where it lands fourth. Named sets are the exception to coloring by count, for the dimensions a reader already has a prior about. A set names hues only. The step stays the chart's call, since a 4px circle on a map and a 40px band on a bar chart want different weights.

heading: Closed sets and catch-all sets
text: The kind decides when a set can claim a chart. | Kind | Claims a chart when | Use it when | | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | | Closed | every key is recognized, and no two hit the same member | the set enumerates a column | | Catch-all | one key is recognized, and the rest go to the sink | the set reads the data | A closed set's members are the only values its column holds, so an unrecognized key means a different column and the set stands down. Two names on one member fail it too, since that draws two slices in one hue. A catch-all set's sink is not a value in the data. A flow diagram might have seven keys of which two are the set's, and folding the rest into one hue is the answer.

heading: The sets
text: A matched key takes the swatch color and the name beside it. A set with a sink member is a catch-all, and the rest are closed.

heading: Naming
text: Use the actual Tailwind class. bg-slate-900, not bg-primary. Semantic aliases go stale the moment a color changes. They also hide the one thing you need when you're looking at a screen and something is off, which is the color that is actually on the element. If you need to express meaning, put it in the component's prop, like for a destructive action.

Most of the type here is working type, the dense UI of an application rather than reading material. So the default is text-sm, not text-base. The scale goes down from there before it goes up. Reach for xs or 2xs when a surface needs to hold more.

heading: Typeface
text: The typeface is Inter, a workhorse drawn for interfaces. It's self-hosted as a variable font across the full 100–900 weight axis, so any weight costs the same as any other.

heading: Scale
text: These are recommendations, not restrictions. Nothing in Tailwind is off the table. 2xl and 4xl are there when a layout needs them. They just don't have a job of their own in the brand. 2xs is the exception. It isn't a Tailwind size at all. It's defined in global.css as a 10px rung below xs, with a 14px line height that matches the shape of the built-in sizes.

heading: Headings in markup
text: Heading levels don't map to fixed sizes. What a level is worth depends on where it sits. As a starting point: | Element | Size | | ------------------------------ | ------ | | h1 on the page background | 3xl | | h1 inside a card | xl | | h2 | xl | | h3 | base |

heading: Responsive
text: Sizes step down below the xl breakpoint, and only at the top of the scale: Large body copy in a hero or marketing section drops a rung the same way, usually base to sm. Everything else holds its size at every width. It's already dense and has nowhere to go.

heading: Weight
text: Body copy is the normal weight. Headings are font-extrabold. Where headings nest and need separating, or where a heading should sit back rather than announce itself, drop to font-semibold. Never all caps.

heading: Leading
text: Leading is set with the relative values, never a fixed pixel height. Four are in use. | Value | Where | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | leading-relaxed | Body copy running to more than one line | | leading-snug | Most headings, and the smaller end of the scale | | leading-tight | Select inputs, badges, and similar compact controls | | leading-none | The largest headings and stat callouts | Headings tighten as they grow. A 5xl stat wants none, and a sm sidebar heading wants snug.

heading: Tracking
text: Inter is drawn tight, which is right at text sizes and wrong at both ends of the scale. Small type opens up so it doesn't clot. Display type closes up so it doesn't drift apart. Tracking is paired to the size tokens in global.css, so it arrives with the size class and there's nothing to remember. text-3xl is already tracked. Tailwind's own scale moves in 0.025em steps, which is too coarse across this range, so the values are graded: | Size | Tracking | | ---------------- | ---------- | | 2xs | 0.015em | | xs | 0.01em | | sm base lg | none | | xl | -0.005em | | 2xl | -0.01em | | 3xl | -0.02em | | 4xl 5xl | -0.03em | Adding a tracking- utility still overrides the paired value, so text-3xl tracking-normal flattens that one heading.

heading: Numerals
text: Numbers are set in tabular figures, applied on body so it holds everywhere. Every digit shares one width, so a column of numbers lines up and a live value doesn't jitter as it changes. Reach for proportional-nums in the rare case a number sits inside running prose and the even spacing looks wrong.

heading: Truncation
text: Dense lists need a hard ceiling on how much room a row can take. In a long list of rows, headings truncate to one line and body copy clamps to two: Everywhere else, let text wrap, and wrap it well. text-balance on headings evens the line lengths so you don't get one orphaned word. text-pretty on body copy does the lighter version of the same thing.

heading: Measure
text: 65 characters is a reasonable ceiling for a paragraph. There isn't much long-form text in the product, so it rarely comes up. It's the number to reach for when it does.

heading: A note on controls
text: Buttons and other controls set their own type and sit a rung below body copy at their default size. That isn't a contradiction. A control has weight, padding, and a fill separating it from everything around it, none of which body copy gets.

Icons come from Font Awesome Pro. Most are solid. A few are regular, like the star, where an outline carries different meaning from solid. An icon is an tag carrying two classes, the variant and the name. Use three styles. Solid is the default. Regular is for the few outlines. Brands is for a third-party logo like fa-shopify. Light, thin, duotone, and sharp stay unused so icons keep one weight across the product. Size and color come from Tailwind utilities rather than Font Awesome's own fa-lg and fa-2x, so an icon moves on the same scale as the text beside it.

heading: Reference
text: Every icon the application uses along with the meaning and usage guidance.

A button is described by one prop. color names the fill. It works out what it is sitting on for itself, by asking the Card or Navbar it's inside. That matters because slate and transparent, the two neutrals, have to stay a step away from their background.

heading: Color
text: The color prop sets the fill. The choices are slate (the default), white, sky, teal, amber, rose, violet, and transparent. Slate is the default because most buttons are ordinary actions that shouldn't compete for attention. Reach for a color only when the button earns it. Sky is the primary action on a screen. Rose is for something destructive. Teal, amber, and violet carry their usual meanings (success, caution, accent). White is the other neutral. Transparent is the quietest option, with no fill until you hover it. White carries no border, so it needs something behind it. Use it on a colored or dark surface, or add shadow to lift it off a white one.

heading: Surface
text: A slate button steps about one level away from whatever it is sitting on. It stays readable without turning into a colored button. | Sitting on | Which is | Slate button | | ------------ | --------------- | ------------ | | default | white | slate-100 | | glass | slate-50 | slate-200 | | sunken | slate-300/30 | slate-300 | | dark | slate-700 | slate-600 | | background | slate-200 | slate-300 | Nobody has to tell it which. A Card and a Navbar announce their surface to everything inside them, slots included, so every button below is passed nothing. The two surfaces missing from the table resolve to ones that are in it. glassRaised reads as glass, and layered as the default white. The last row is the page itself, the one surface with no component to announce it. That's what sitsOn is for. An element that paints its own background can wrap its contents in SurfaceProvider instead. A button with nothing above it assumes white, so a bare one on the page comes out slate-100 on slate-200, which is hard to see and easy to miss. Everything else ignores the question. Sky, teal, amber, rose, violet, and white hold their value on every background. The five accents rest at 300, which separates them from any neutral behind them.

heading: Size
text: The size prop controls height, padding, and corner radius. The sizes are xs, sm, md (the default), lg, and xl.

heading: Outline
text: outline drops the fill and keeps the border. A faint wash of the fill comes back on hover. The label stays black, which reads on any light surface. On dark it switches to white, since black on the panel would be 2.0:1. With no fill of its own to read against, it's the shape that most depends on knowing where it is.

heading: Shadow
text: shadow adds a resting shadow that deepens on hover.

heading: Loading and disabled
text: loading swaps the label for a spinner while keeping the button's width. disabled fades the button and blocks pointer events, for both button and link variants.

heading: Block
text: block makes the button fill the width of its container.

heading: Two buttons
text: When a card, the floating action panel, or a modal's action bar ends in two buttons, the primary action goes on the right and fills the width. Give it block and write it last. The secondary button sits on the left at its own width.

heading: Link
text: Pass an href to render an instead of a . Styling is identical.

A card is the panel most of the interface is built from. The surface prop says where the panel sits in the stack, and the card announces that to everything inside it. A Button in a card takes the right neutral without being told anything.

heading: Surface
text: Content is passed as children. The surface prop sets the background. The choices are default, glass, glassRaised, layered, sunken, and dark. The two composite surfaces pass on what a button in them can actually see. glassRaised passes on glass, and layered passes on the default white.

heading: A surface that isn't a card
text: Anything else that paints a background of its own is a surface to the eye and silent to the code. SurfaceProvider is how it speaks up. It renders one element, so it can be the box carrying the background instead of another layer around it. The navbar's dropdown panel is the one use in the system. It is white whatever the bar is, so its buttons take slate-100 instead of the slate-600 they would inherit from a dark bar. Reach for it only where there's a real background. Wrapping something that paints nothing tells the buttons inside it a lie, and they have no way to check.

heading: Padding
text: The padding prop sets the inset. The choices are none, compact (p-4), default (p-6), and spacious (p-8). Use none when the card wraps content that manages its own spacing, such as a table or an image.

heading: Element
text: The as prop sets the tag the card renders as. It defaults to div, which is right for a card that is only a visual grouping. Switch to section when the card is a titled region of the page, or article when its content would still make sense pulled out on its own. Under the layered surface the tag lands on the card holding the content. The offset layers behind it stay presentational.

heading: Interaction
text: Cards have no hover or active styles, deliberately. A hover state would move the card off the rung its surface is documented at in Color, and it would light half the screen without saying where to aim. When a card is meant to link somewhere or perform an action, put a Button inside it and let the button do that work. Make it the card's primary button, so there is one obvious target instead of a panel that might be clickable somewhere. The button is also the part that takes keyboard focus and the part a screen reader announces as pressable, neither of which a card can do. This holds for list rows too. A row of results is a stack of cards, and the thing you click is the link or button inside the row, not the row itself.

A badge labels the thing next to it, such as a status, a count, or a category. It is a pill of text and nothing else. It doesn't respond to hover and it isn't clickable, so anything you can press is a Button, not a badge. A badge sits on the label weight from Color: a 100 fill, a 900 label, a 300 border, and a 500 icon. Contrast has the numbers.

heading: Color
text: The color prop sets the tint. The choices are sky (the default), teal, amber, rose, violet, and slate. The meanings come from Color. Teal is success or completion. Amber is caution. Rose is failing or destructive. Sky is the primary thing on the screen. Violet is an accent with no status attached. Slate has no meaning at all, and it should stay the answer for most badges. A colored badge in every row of a table spends the color budget on something nobody is reading. A badge carries a fill and a border of its own, so it holds the same values on every surface. Unlike a Button, it never has to know what it is sitting on. Every surface a badge lands on is a light one. The dark card is the app navigation bar, and nothing in there is badged.

heading: Extending the range
text: Seven more tints sit outside the palette. They are lime, orange, green, blue, fuchsia, pink, and emerald. They run on the same tint as everything else, so the treatment doesn't change. Use them only where you need to extend the range of difference between badges. A chart legend whose keys are badges needs as many distinguishable values as the chart has series. A table column of tags, where a team has defined thirty of their own, needs the same thing. In both cases the job is telling one badge from the next, not saying what any of them means. Everywhere else, use the accents. These seven carry no meaning, and next to an accent they borrow one they don't have. Emerald beside teal reads as a second kind of success. Orange beside amber reads as a worse warning. Taken in this order, each color is as far from the ones already on screen as the set allows. Past eight categories, reconsider whether color is carrying the distinction at all. A label, an icon, or a sorted order will do it better than a fourteenth green.

heading: Size
text: The size prop controls height, padding, and text size. The sizes are 2xs, xs, sm, md (the default), and lg. xs is the size to reach for inside something dense, like a table row, a list item, or a card header. A taller pill there pushes the line around it apart. That's most badges in the app. Drop to 2xs for a badge riding alongside small text. Reach for lg only when the badge is the subject rather than an annotation.

heading: Icons
text: Icons go in the slot next to the label. They don't inherit the label's size. They are carefully sized for visual balance. Don't guess, look at the component. They also take the 500 of the badge's color rather than the 900 the label uses. The same badge at every size: The 500 is decorative, at 1.9:1 to 3.7:1 on its own tint, so the icon can reinforce the label but never replace it. An icon with no label isn't a badge. It's an icon in a pill, and a plain icon would do the job better.

heading: Contrast
text: Every color clears WCAG AAA and APCA's Lc 75 mark for body text. | Fill | Label | WCAG 2.x | APCA | | ----------- | ----------- | -------- | ------ | | sky-100 | sky-900 | 8.2:1 | Lc 82 | | teal-100 | teal-900 | 8.4:1 | Lc 83 | | amber-100 | amber-900 | 8.2:1 | Lc 83 | | rose-100 | rose-900 | 8.0:1 | Lc 78 | | violet-100 | violet-900 | 9.3:1 | Lc 83 | | slate-100 | slate-900 | 16.3:1 | Lc 98 | Badge text runs 10–12px, the size at which a contrast shortfall counts most, so the margin matters. Color has the comparison with the control rung. The extended set lands in the same band: | Fill | Label | WCAG 2.x | APCA | | ----------- | ------------ | -------- | ----- | | lime-100 | lime-900 | 8.0:1 | Lc 84 | | orange-100 | orange-900 | 8.2:1 | Lc 82 | | green-100 | green-900 | 8.3:1 | Lc 84 | | blue-100 | blue-900 | 8.5:1 | Lc 80 | | fuchsia-100 | fuchsia-900 | 8.7:1 | Lc 82 | | pink-100 | pink-900 | 8.2:1 | Lc 80 | | emerald-100 | emerald-900 | 8.5:1 | Lc 83 |

heading: What the tint costs
text: A 100 fill barely separates from the surface (rose-100 on slate-200 is 1.02:1), so the 300 border is part of the treatment and there is no option to drop it. | Element | On white | On the page background | | ----------- | -------- | ---------------------- | | sky-100 | 1.15:1 | 1.07:1 | | teal-100 | 1.13:1 | 1.09:1 | | amber-100 | 1.11:1 | 1.11:1 | | rose-100 | 1.20:1 | 1.02:1 | | violet-100 | 1.19:1 | 1.04:1 | | slate-100 | 1.10:1 | 1.12:1 | | sky-300 | 1.67:1 | 1.35:1 | | rose-300 | 1.92:1 | 1.56:1 | | slate-300 | 1.48:1 | 1.21:1 | Even with the border, nothing here reaches the 3:1 WCAG asks of a control's boundary, which is fine for something that isn't a control. The label carries the meaning. Never build a badge whose meaning depends on someone noticing the fill.

The navigation bar is the entry point into the application. Main navigation and frequently used actions both live here. Navigation sits on the left, with the two most used page links called out as buttons. The right side holds account-level options like team and group switching, kiosk mode, and settings. A screen has one navbar, never two. It is the only place the dark surface from Card is used. The component is one wrapper and two sub-components. Navbar is the bar itself, and it decides how much of the navigation fits. NavbarAction sits inside Navbar and holds either a link or a label with a dropdown menu. NavbarActionItem is a row inside a dropdown. Actions go in the default slot because the bar measures them. The row is a and each section is an , so a screen reader announces how many there are. NavbarAction renders that for you. Everything in the default slot should be a NavbarAction. A Button dropped straight into the row would be a in a with no around it, and it wouldn't be measured or folded. Put it inside an action instead. The list rule applies inside menus too. The items slot is a list, so anything in it that isn't a NavbarActionItem needs its own . Outside a list, such as the bar's right slot, pass as="div" so the action renders a instead. The bar is 64px tall, and 80px once it has the room for it. There's no short variant. Anything that has to be shorter is a toolbar, like an inbox switcher or a builder's toolbar.

heading: Examples
text: Every bar below is live. They run at the width of this column rather than a window, so they hold fewer sections than the real bar does. Folding explains why. Open the menus. Open full screen under any bar puts it across the top of the window, where resizing exercises the fold. Which bar is open is in the URL, so a link to a preview can be sent to someone. The two bars under Surface carry Message Hub and Quick Blast, as the product's bar does. Those two outrank the sections for room, which is why both bars are down to a hamburger in a column this narrow. The other examples leave them off.

heading: Surface
text: The surface prop says which surface the bar is. The choices are dark (the default) and glass. Both are named after the Card surface they are, and both are surfaces Button knows how to sit on. {/ An open panel hangs out of the bar's box, so a demo has to out-rank the one under it or that one paints over the menu. isolate on every demo keeps a bar's own z-30 from reaching the page, which is what lets the two demos with something below them be the only numbers here. /} dark is slate-700 and it's what the product ships. glass is slate-50, without the border the Card surface carries, since a bar is edge to edge. The prop sets the bar's background and announces it to everything inside the bar, side slots included. A section is a transparent Button, so it reads its label color and its hover fill off the surface the same way a filled button does: white on the dark bar, black on the glass one, hovering one step off whichever it's on. A Button in #right is on the bar's surface without being told.

heading: Sections
text: A NavbarAction is either a link or a menu, and the arrow at its end says which. Give it an href and it renders an with an arrow pointing right. Give it an items slot and it renders a with a chevron. That chevron opens a panel underneath, and points up for as long as the panel is showing. hideArrow drops the arrow if a particular action is better off without one. The rows in an items slot are NavbarActionItems. Give a row an href and it renders an . Leave it off and it renders a . For a panel that isn't a list of rows, use the dropdown slot instead of items and put whatever you like in it. The bar draws the panel and its slab and leaves the inside to you. The team button at the right of the examples above is built that way. icon takes Font Awesome classes as a string, like icon="fa-solid fa-robot", and sets them on an ahead of the label. In the bars above, open More. The chevrons are the menus, and Support is the one with an arrow. A menu drops from the left edge of its action. placement="right" lines it up with the right edge instead, which is what anything near the right end of the bar needs. Under 40rem the setting is ignored, since a menu takes the full width of the bar there.

heading: An action around your own control
text: Put a Button or a link in an action's label and the action stops being the control. It renders a , draws no arrow, and lets what's inside take the focus, the cursor, and the press. This is the shape the side slots use, and the only way to put a button in an action, since a button can't sit inside a button. The action still positions the panel, carries the marker, and toggles the menu when the control is pressed. It can't put anything inside your control, so three things move to you: the chevron, aria-haspopup, and aria-expanded. The label slot hands you open for all three: The explicit #default template is what lets the slot be destructured. An action whose label is a bare word needs none of this. The space around the control takes no cursor and no click, so the press lands on the control and nowhere else.

heading: The current section
text: active on an action marks the section you're in, with a sky-500 bar under the label. active on an item does the same for a row in the open menu, as a bar down the left edge of the panel. {/ The open panel is positioned, so it adds no height of its own. The margin is what keeps it off the paragraph underneath. /} Mark exactly one action active. The marker is the only thing on the bar that says where you are (the label doesn't change color), so a second one makes it say nothing. Mark the thing you're actually on and the bar works out the rest. An action whose menu holds what's marked takes the marker itself, including More when the marked section has folded into it. Hovering a section says so with the button's own fill, not with a bar under it. The marker is for where you are and nothing else, so the two cues are never confused for each other. :marker="false" turns the marker off for a single action. It's there for something that sits on the bar without being a place you can be. While a menu is open, its panel covers the marker under it, as in the bar above. The open panel says where you are instead. Under 40rem there is no panel to say it, so the hamburger takes a slate bar while its menu is open: slate-500 on the dark bar, slate-300 on the glass one.

heading: Menus inside menus
text: Put a NavbarAction inside an items slot and it becomes a section of that menu rather than a second panel, a heading with its own rows indented under it. In a bar wider than 40rem those sections are open. In a narrower bar they collapse, and the chevron flips as they open. A collapsed section holding the current page takes the page's bar onto its own heading, and gives it back to the row when opened. The account menu on the right of the examples above is built this way. Settings and Teams are actions nested inside one action. Two levels is the limit in practice. Nothing in the component stops a third, but at that point the thing you're building is a page, not a menu.

heading: Left and right
text: #left holds the logo and #right holds the account. Neither is measured and neither folds, so what you put there stays on the bar. Keep each slot to one or two things, since every pixel a side slot takes is a pixel the sections don't get. The bars at the top of this page carry two more things on the left: Message Hub and Quick Blast, the actions the product wants a click away from anywhere. They go in the slot as buttons rather than in the row as sections, so they never fold into More. On the right, the team you're in ends the bar. It's the one thing that never moves at any width, because which account you're looking at is not something to leave anyone guessing about. What's in a side slot outranks every section. The bar will put all five sections behind one More button before either of these buttons gives up a pixel. That's the right order for these two, since they're what the product is for, and the reason to think twice about a third. Under 40rem the bar folds every section away and hands a narrow flag to both side slots and to the two menu slots below. It moves nothing of yours on its own. The examples answer the flag by keeping the logo, the menu, and the team on the bar and sending the rest into the menu.

heading: Moving into the menu
text: #nested-before and #nested-after add rows at the top and the bottom of the More menu, around whatever sections have folded into it. With narrow, they're how something leaves the bar without leaving the page: It's written twice because a slot is markup, and the bar can't hand the same markup to two slots. Take any bar on this page to a phone and it holds the logo, one menu, and the team. Open the menu and the two buttons are at the top, with Settings, Teams, and Log out below the sections.

heading: Folding
text: The bar decides how many sections fit and puts the rest behind one menu. It measures rather than using breakpoints, because the answer depends on the labels, the side slots, and the reader's font size. Under 40rem it doesn't measure. Every section goes into the menu whether or not one would fit, and the side slots get narrow. Widening out of it gives back what the side slots moved first, and the sections after. Above that it measures its own width, not the window's, so a bar in a column, a split pane, or beside a collapsible sidebar folds to the room it actually has. Its spacing is a container query for the same reason. It refolds on its own when a label changes, a section is added or removed, a font finishes loading, or the reader turns their text size up. There is nothing to call. Whatever goes in the default slot is mounted twice, once on the bar or in the menu and once hidden for measuring. A NavbarAction doesn't notice. Something that fires a request or starts a timer when it mounts would do it twice, and doesn't belong on the bar. It takes sections from the left while they fit, and what's left goes into a More menu at the end of the row as nested actions. If everything fits there's no More button at all. The exception is a menu carrying something of its own from #nested-before or #nested-after, which is on the row at every width and counted like a section. One section left on the bar turns into no sections. A lone section beside More would read as the whole navigation, so the last one folds too and the trigger becomes a hamburger. There is nothing to tune. How tightly the bar packs isn't a setting, because the measurement already has the answer. Open this one full screen and drag the window in and out to watch the count change:

heading: Interaction
text: A menu opens on click. It closes on a click anywhere outside it, on Escape, or on a second click of its own label. open is two-way. Bind it with v-model:open to drive a menu from outside, or pass it one-way to open a menu on load. Everything on the bar is a real or . The whole bar is reachable with Tab, a menu opens with Enter, and its rows join the tab order once it's open. An action that is its own control carries aria-haspopup and an aria-expanded that tracks its panel. One wrapped around a control of yours can't, since the attributes belong on the control. It hands you open on the label slot to set them from. aria-current goes on the action or item that really is the page, and only there. An action marked because its menu holds the current page takes the marker without the attribute. There are no arrow keys and no role="menu", deliberately. This is a disclosure pattern, a row of buttons each revealing a list of links, with Tab moving through everything. role="menu" would commit the bar to menubar semantics, which are for application menus, not navigation. Closing a menu with Escape hands focus back to the control that opened it. A section that folds while it has focus passes that focus to the More button. Menus don't open on hover. A pointer crossing the bar would open them by accident, and a touchscreen has no hover at all.

heading: Contrast
text: The bar's own pairings are the strongest in the system. White on slate-700 is 10.4:1, and the glass bar's black on slate-50 is 20.1:1. Menus are darker still, since a panel is white and its rows are slate-900. Color explains the two columns. | Element | On | WCAG 2.x | APCA | | ------------------------- | ---------- | -------- | ------ | | white label | slate-700 | 10.4:1 | Lc 98 | | black label | slate-50 | 20.1:1 | Lc 106 | | slate-900 menu row | white | 17.8:1 | Lc 105 | | slate-900 menu row hover | sky-100 | 15.5:1 | Lc 95 | | sky-500 marker | slate-700 | 3.8:1 | Lc 40 | | slate-400 icon | slate-700 | 3.9:1 | Lc 41 | | slate-500 open marker | slate-700 | 2.2:1 | Lc 19 | | slate-300 open marker | slate-50 | 1.4:1 | Lc 20 | | sky-500 item bar | white | 2.7:1 | Lc 40 | The labels are the part that has to be read, and they have room to spare. Everything below them is a marker or an icon, and those are priced differently. WCAG asks 3:1 of a non-text element that carries meaning, not the 4.5:1 it asks of text. The section marker clears that at 3.8:1, and the icons at 3.9:1. Icons drop to 2.5:1 on the glass bar, but they're never the only thing saying what a section is. An action with an icon and no label is a guess. The two open markers are far under, at 2.2:1 and 1.4:1, and that's fine for a bar that only exists while the menu it belongs to is on screen saying the same thing. The item bar is the one that can't carry its own weight. At 2.7:1 against the panel it's just under the 3:1 a state indicator wants, so it isn't asked to work alone. The current row's label is also semibold, which survives at any contrast, and aria-current carries the same thing to a screen reader. That pairing is the rule to keep if you build on this. A state that exists only as a color a shade off its background is a state some people can't see.

A select is a native in the house shell. The picker that opens is the platform's, so it behaves the way it does everywhere else on the device. Options come from the options prop, or from the default slot when you need or anything the prop can't express. A select usually sits on a glass Card or on the page background. Almost never on a white default card. The exception is a white card nested inside another card. Anything that looks like a select is held to the same rules, whether or not it is one. A hand-written in site chrome, or a button that opens a menu and is drawn as a field, takes the select's height, radius, padding, edge, chevron, and focus ring at the size it matches. Reach for the component first. Where it can't be the component, copy the select at one of its sizes rather than approximating it. How a field goes together with its label, its description, and its messages is on the Forms page.

heading: Label and description
text: label is what the select is for, and every select in a form column gets one. description is a second line under it, for what the label can't hold. Both render above the control, and the label is wired to the select with for. Leaving label off is how a compact field is written, and that's the only place it's right.

heading: Options
text: The options prop takes an array of { value, label }. An option can also carry disabled. Write the options as markup instead when you need grouping, or a first option that stands in for no choice at all. The value is bound with v-model. Anything else you pass, such as name or required, lands on the rather than the wrapper around it. An id of your own lands there too, and the label points at it.

heading: Surface
text: A select works out what it is sitting on for itself, by asking the Card or Navbar it's inside. The white fill holds on every surface. What draws the boundary is what changes. | Sitting on | Which is | Boundary | | ------------ | ------------ | ----------------- | | default | white | slate-200 border | | glass | slate-50 | slate-200 border | | sunken | slate-300/30 | shadow, no border | | dark | slate-700 | shadow, no border | | background | slate-200 | shadow, no border | White and glass get the border. Sunken, dark, and the page background get the shadow and no border. Glass is a step off white, close enough that a border still reads as the edge. From sunken down the shadow does that job, and a border would only double it. The page background is the one surface with no component to announce it. That's what sitsOn is for. An element that paints a background of its own can wrap its contents in SurfaceProvider instead.

heading: Size
text: The size prop sets height, padding, and text size. The sizes are xs, sm, md (the default), lg, and xl. They match Button at every step, so a select and a button in the same row are the same height and share a corner radius. Text runs text-xs at xs and sm, text-sm at md and lg, and text-base at xl.

heading: Width
text: A select is as wide as its longest option. Add block to fill the container instead, which is what a select in a form column wants.

heading: Error and hint
text: error takes the message to show under the control. Passing it recolors the border, the text, and the chevron, marks the line with a warning icon, and points aria-describedby at the message. The border is there in the resting state too, so only its color changes and nothing moves when a form fails validation. On the page background the resting border is transparent rather than absent, for the same reason. hint is the same line before anything goes wrong, at slate-600 behind an info mark. A select can show both.

heading: Disabled
text: disabled swaps the white fill for slate-100 with slate-500 text. On a shadowed surface the shadow goes and a slate-200 border takes over, so the control still has an edge.

heading: Interaction
text: On a shadowed surface, hover deepens the shadow from shadow to shadow-md. On white and glass there is no shadow, so hover does nothing. There is no press state either, because the press opens the platform picker and the picker is what gives the feedback. Focus draws a blue outline, two pixels wide at a two pixel offset, and only for keyboard focus. Clicking the control doesn't ring it. Everything else is the browser's. Space or Enter opens the list, the arrow keys move through it, and typing jumps to a matching option.

heading: Contrast
text: | Element | On | WCAG 2.x | | ---------- | ---------- | -------- | | slate-900 | white | 17.8:1 | | slate-800 | glass | 14.0:1 | | slate-500 | glass | 4.6:1 | | rose-600 | white | 4.5:1 | | rose-800 | glass | 7.6:1 | | slate-500 | white | 4.8:1 | | slate-200 | white | 1.2:1 | | slate-300 | white | 1.5:1 | | rose-300 | white | 1.9:1 | | white fill | glass | 1.05:1 | | white fill | background | 1.23:1 | The option text and the error message clear AA comfortably. The label is slate-800 and clears it by a wide margin. The chevron sits at slate-500, which clears AA at 4.8:1, and it is decorative in any case. The description is slate-500 too, which holds on white and glass and falls to 3.9:1 on the page background. The boundary doesn't. The border runs 1.2:1 against the white fill, well short of the 3:1 WCAG asks of a control's boundary. The fill itself is only 1.05:1 against a glass card. On the page background the fill separates a little better at 1.23:1, with the shadow to help. The error state has the same problem, at 1.9:1 for the rose-300 border, which is why the message under the control carries the meaning rather than the color.

An input is the text field, and the textarea. Passing rows turns it into the other. A textarea grows with what's typed into it, with no prop to ask for that. It follows Select for everything around the edge. A white fill, a slate-200 border on white and glass, and a shadow with no border on sunken, dark, and the page background. It works that out from the Card it's inside, or from sitsOn where there's no card to ask. Like a select, it belongs on a glass card or on the page background rather than on a white one. An input fills the width it's given. Constrain it from the outside, with the column it sits in. Anything that looks like an input is held to the same rules, whether or not it is one. A button styled as a search field, like the one that opens the search palette in this site's sidebar, takes the input's height, radius, padding, edge, and focus ring at the size it matches. Reach for the component first. Where it can't be the component, copy the input at one of its sizes rather than approximating it. How a field goes together with its label, its description, and its messages is on the Forms page.

heading: Label and description
text: label is what the field is for, and every field in a form column gets one. description is a second line under it, for what the label can't hold. Both render above the control, and the label is wired to the field with for, so clicking it focuses. Leaving label off is how a compact field is written, and that's the only place it's right. Avoid placeholder everywhere else, since a field with grey text in it reads as a field that's already answered.

heading: Type
text: The type prop is passed through to the field. The choices are text (the default), password, number, email, tel, url, search, time, date, and datetime-local. number and password do more than pass the type along. They have their own sections below.

heading: Surface
text: An input works out what it is sitting on for itself, by asking the Card or Navbar it's inside. The fill stays white. The edge follows the Select rule, a slate-200 border on white and glass, and a shadow with no border on sunken, dark, and the page background. Pass sitsOn on the page background, since nothing there can announce it. An element that paints a background of its own can wrap its contents in SurfaceProvider instead.

heading: Size
text: The size prop sets height, padding, and text size. The sizes are xs, sm, md (the default), lg, and xl. They match Button and Select at every step. On a textarea the size sets vertical padding instead of a height, since rows and the content are what decide how tall it is.

heading: Content inside the field
text: Three slots put things inside the field, and the value's padding is measured off whatever you put in them. left and right sit over the fill. box is a filled panel pinned to the start, for a unit or a prefix that is part of the value rather than a decoration. box and left are mutually exclusive. When both are passed, the box wins and the left slot isn't rendered.

heading: More than one line
text: rows renders a textarea, at the height it names. Any value counts, so rows={1} is a field that starts at one line. From there it grows with its content and caps at half the viewport height, unless maxHeight says otherwise. At one row a textarea is exactly as tall as an input of the same size, and each row after that adds one line. The growing is field-sizing: content, so it's the browser doing it rather than anything measuring the content. There's nothing to turn on. Browsers without that property can't grow the field, so they get the drag handle instead. Where the property is supported there is no handle, since the field is already sizing itself.

heading: Numbers
text: type="number" runs as a text field underneath, so the value can be cleaned up as it's typed. Anything that isn't a number is dropped, the minus sign only counts at the start, and the decimals are held to whatever step implies. min and max clamp on blur, which is also when the value is padded out to the step's decimals. The stepper appears on focus and disappears again, so a row of numeric fields isn't a wall of arrows. ↑ and ↓ do the same job and are always there, which is why the buttons are out of the tab order. A right slot replaces the stepper.

heading: Passwords
text: type="password" with togglePassword adds the reveal button. The button is in the tab order and it announces which state it will switch to, so the reveal is reachable without a mouse.

heading: Error
text: error takes one message or an array of them. Passing it recolors the border and the text, marks the line with a warning icon, and points aria-describedby at the messages. There's an error slot too, for a message that needs markup, such as a link to whatever the reader has to go and fix.

heading: Hint
text: hint is the line under the field that is there before anything goes wrong. It sits at slate-600 behind an info mark, and stays put when an error appears above it.

heading: Counting characters
text: counter swaps the hint area for a Char Counter. It needs maxlength to count against. Passing counter stops maxlength and minlength reaching the field, so someone can type past the limit and see that they have, rather than finding the field silently refusing keystrokes. The counter is muted while the field is unfocused.

heading: Disabled
text: disabled swaps the white fill for slate-100 with slate-500 text.

heading: Interaction
text: Focus draws a blue outline, two pixels wide at a two pixel offset. Unlike a Button, a text field takes the ring on a click as well as on a keyboard focus, because that's what :focus-visible does for a field you can type into. On a shadowed surface, hover deepens the shadow from shadow to shadow-md. On white and glass there's no shadow, so hover does nothing. The numeric stepper and the counter both key off focus. The stepper fades in, and the counter comes out of its muted state.

heading: Contrast
text: The values are the same as Select, and so are the shortfalls. The border is short of the 3:1 WCAG asks of a control's boundary, and the message under the field is what carries an error rather than the rose border. Three colors are the input's own. The label runs slate-800, at 14.6:1 on white and 11.9:1 on the page background. The hint runs slate-600, at 7.6:1 on white and 6.1:1 on the page background. The box is slate-600 on a slate-100 fill, at 6.9:1. All three clear AA on every surface. The description is the one that doesn't. It runs slate-500, which is 4.8:1 on white and 4.6:1 on glass, and 3.9:1 on the page background. Description text is never large enough for the 3:1 threshold, so a field on the page background with a description is short of AA. Put fields that need a description on a glass card.

A char counter is the bar and the count under a field that has a limit. Input renders one for you when you pass counter, so reach for this directly only when the thing being counted isn't an input. content is what to measure and max is what to measure it against. content takes a string or an array, so a list of recipients counts the same way a message does.

heading: Filling up
text: The bar is the length over max, and it holds slate until the count is worth reacting to. Amber is the last tenth before the limit, and rose is past it. maxWarning moves where amber starts. Nothing stops at the limit, since the counter reports and the field decides.

heading: Counting up to a minimum
text: min and minWarning cover the other direction, for a field that is too short rather than too long. Below min the counter reads as an error. Below minWarning it warns.

heading: Muted
text: muted holds the bar and the count at slate whatever the length is. Input passes it while the field is unfocused, so a form of counters isn't a row of warnings before anyone has typed.

heading: Label
text: label names what is being counted. It defaults to characters.

heading: Contrast
text: | Element | On | WCAG 2.x | | --------- | ----- | -------- | | slate-500 | white | 4.8:1 | | rose-800 | white | 7.9:1 | The count clears AA at slate-500, and the part that turns rose clears it at 7.9:1. The bar itself is decorative. Amber and rose there repeat what the count already says, so nothing is carried by the color alone.

A checkbox is a native with a drawn box beside its label. The input itself is there, hidden to the eye and not to the browser, so it submits with a form, answers to Space, and announces itself as a checkbox. The whole row is the target. The box, the label, and the description are inside one , so a press anywhere in them toggles the box. How a field goes together with its label, its description, and its messages is on the Forms page.

heading: Label and description
text: label is the option text, and it sits beside the box rather than above it. description is a second line under the label, for what the label can't hold. Use the default slot instead of label when the text needs markup. The label is font-medium and slate-800, a step lighter than the extrabold label on an Input. A checkbox label is the answer rather than the question.

heading: One box or several
text: Bind v-model to a boolean for a single box that stands on its own. Bind it to an array for a set, and give each box a value. Checking one adds its value to the array, unchecking takes it out. A set gets a and a , so the question above the options is read out with each of them. Stack the boxes with gap-2, or gap-3 when they carry descriptions.

heading: Boxed
text: boxed draws the row as a bordered box that fills its container, the same form a Radio takes for a set of options. The box rests transparent with a slate-300 border, so the surface shows through, and goes white with a sky-500 border when checked. The marker centers on the block rather than on the first line. Stack boxed rows with gap-2. Everything else on this page applies to a boxed checkbox as well. Error recolors the box's border along with the marker, disabled quiets the label, and the sizes set the padding along with the marker. On the page background the marker inside the box drops its shadow.

heading: Indeterminate
text: indeterminate draws a dash instead of a check, for a box that stands for a set where only some are on. It's a display state. The model isn't touched until someone presses the box, and then it's the press you handle.

heading: Surface
text: A checkbox works out what it is sitting on for itself, by asking the Card or Navbar it's inside. An unchecked box is white on white and glass. On sunken, dark, and the page background it has no fill, so the surface shows through it. Its boundary changes with the surface too. A checked box is sky-300 with a sky-500 border on every surface. | Sitting on | Which is | Boundary | | ------------ | ------------ | ----------------- | | default | white | slate-300 border | | glass | slate-50 | slate-300 border | | sunken | slate-300/30 | slate-400 border | | dark | slate-700 | slate-500 border | | background | slate-200 | slate-400 border | The label goes white on the dark surface, and the description slate-300. Everywhere else they are slate-800 and slate-500. A boxed checkbox takes the same border as its marker, except on dark, where the box drops to slate-900. The marker inside it never carries the shadow. Checked, the box goes white on every surface but dark, where it goes slate-800 so the white label stays readable. The page background is the only surface that gets the shadow. That's what sitsOn is for, since nothing on the page background can announce it. An element that paints a background of its own can wrap its contents in SurfaceProvider instead.

heading: Size
text: The size prop sets the box, the label, and the gap between them. The sizes are sm, md (the default), and lg. The box is the line-height of its own label at every size, so the two line up on the first line however far the text wraps. There is no xs or xl. Input, Select, and Button run the full five, and a checkbox stops at the three that stay big enough to hit.

heading: Error and hint
text: error takes the message to show under the row. It recolors the border, marks the line with a warning icon, sets aria-invalid, and points aria-describedby at the message. Pass an array for more than one message. The border is there in the resting state too, so only its color changes and nothing moves when a form fails validation. hint is the same line before anything goes wrong, at slate-600 behind an info mark. A checkbox can show both.

heading: Disabled
text: disabled fills the box slate-100 and drops the label to slate-500. A checked box that's disabled keeps its check, in slate-400, rather than losing the state along with the control.

heading: Interaction
text: On the page background, hovering anywhere in the row deepens the shadow from shadow to shadow-md. On a panel there is no shadow, so hover does nothing. Pressing shrinks the box to 90% for the length of the press, and leaves the label where it is. The shrink is motion-safe, so it doesn't run for someone who has asked for reduced motion. Focus draws a blue outline around the box, two pixels wide at a two pixel offset, and only for keyboard focus. Pressing the row doesn't ring it. A boxed checkbox draws the outline around the whole row instead, and its border steps one shade darker on hover. Everything else is the browser's. Tab reaches the box and Space toggles it. Boxes in a set are each their own tab stop, unlike a set of radios.

heading: Contrast

Sky-300 against a white card is 1.7:1, and the sky-500 border that edges it is 2.7:1, both short of the 3:1 WCAG asks of a control's boundary. A radio is a native with a drawn dot beside its label. The input itself is there, hidden to the eye and not to the browser, so it submits with a form, answers to the arrow keys, and announces itself as a radio. A radio never stands alone. Two or more share one v-model and one name, and the model holds the value of whichever is picked. The name is what makes them a group to the browser, and without it the arrow keys won't move between them. Most groups are boxed, which draws each option as a bordered row filling the width of its container. The bare radio is for a set that sits inside something else, like a table row or a dense settings list. A Radio Bar lays a set out in one line, each option a label in a shared track the height of an Input. How a field goes together with its label, its description, and its messages is on the Forms page.

heading: Boxed
text: boxed draws the row as a bordered box that fills its container. The box rests transparent with a slate-300 border, so the surface shows through, and goes white with a sky-500 border when picked. The circle centers on the block rather than on the first line, so a description pushes it down to the middle of the row. Stack boxed rows with gap-2. Everything else on this page applies to a boxed radio as well. Error recolors the box's border along with the circle, disabled quiets the label, and the sizes set the padding along with the circle.

heading: A group
text: Each radio carries the value it puts in the model when it's picked. Wrap the set in a with a , so the question above the options is read out with each of them. Stack them with gap-2, or gap-3 when they carry descriptions. Picking one unpicks the rest. Nothing in the component does that, since the browser does it for every input sharing a name.

heading: Label and description
text: label is the option text, and it sits beside the dot rather than above it. description is a second line under the label, for what the label can't hold. Use the default slot instead of label when the text needs markup. The label is font-medium and slate-800, a step lighter than the extrabold label on an Input. A radio label is the answer rather than the question. The question is the legend above the group.

heading: Surface
text: A radio works out what it is sitting on for itself, by asking the Card or Navbar it's inside. The circle is white on white and glass. On sunken, dark, and the page background it has no fill, so the surface shows through it. Its border changes with the surface too. Picking it swaps the border for a sky-500 ring and lands a sky-500 dot inside. | Sitting on | Which is | Boundary | | ------------ | ------------ | ----------------- | | default | white | slate-300 border | | glass | slate-50 | slate-300 border | | sunken | slate-300/30 | slate-400 border | | dark | slate-700 | slate-500 border | | background | slate-200 | slate-400 border | The label goes white on the dark surface, and the description slate-300. Everywhere else they are slate-800 and slate-500. A boxed radio takes the same border as its circle, except on dark, where the box drops to slate-900. Picked, the box goes white on every surface but dark, where it goes slate-800 so the white label stays readable. A radio carries no shadow on any surface, so its border runs a step darker than a Checkbox's to hold against the surface, and the page background takes a border like the rest of them. That's what sitsOn is for, since nothing on the page background can announce it. An element that paints a background of its own can wrap its contents in SurfaceProvider instead.

heading: Size
text: The size prop sets the circle, the label, and the gap between them. The sizes are sm, md (the default), and lg, at 12, 16, and 20px. A Checkbox runs 16, 20, and 24px under the same names. The ring is 2px at md and lg, and 1px at sm, where a 2px ring would leave the dot no gap around it.

heading: Error and hint
text: error takes the message to show under the row. It recolors the border, marks the line with a warning icon, sets aria-invalid, and points aria-describedby at the message. Pass an array for more than one message. A group has one answer, so it has one message. Put error on the last radio in the set, where the line reads as the group's own. hint is the same line before anything goes wrong, at slate-600 behind an info mark. A radio can show both.

heading: Disabled
text: disabled fills the circle slate-100 and drops the label to slate-500. A picked radio that's disabled keeps its dot, in slate-400, rather than losing the answer along with the control.

heading: Interaction
text: Nothing happens on hover. A radio has no shadow to deepen. Pressing shrinks the circle to 90% for the length of the press, and leaves the label where it is. The shrink is motion-safe, so it doesn't run for someone who has asked for reduced motion. Focus draws a blue outline around the circle, two pixels wide at a two pixel offset, and only for keyboard focus. Pressing the row doesn't ring it. A boxed radio draws the outline around the box instead, and its border steps one shade darker on hover. Everything else is the browser's. A group is one tab stop, landing on whichever radio is picked. The arrow keys move through the set and pick as they go, wrapping at either end.

The dot being there is what carries the answer, and a dot is a shape rather than a color, so the state survives without it. The colors themselves don't clear. Sky-500 against a white card is 2.7:1 for the ring and for the dot, short of the 3:1 WCAG asks of a control's boundary. The unpicked circle has the same problem at 1.5:1, and so does the rose-300 error border at 1.9:1, which is why the message under the row carries the error rather than the color. The ring thickens when the radio is picked, at md and lg, so the weight moves as well as the color. The disabled dot runs slate-400 on slate-100 at 2.4:1. Disabled controls are exempt from the contrast rules, and it is deliberately quiet.

A radio bar is a set of Radio options laid out in one line, inside a bordered track the height of an Input. Each option drops its circle and draws as a centered label, and the picked one sits on a slate-200 pill. The radios inside are the same component as everywhere else, so they keep their name, their value, their v-model, and the browser's arrow keys. The bar fills the width of its container, and the options space out evenly across it, with the same gap at the edges as between them. A bar next to an Input of the same size sits level with it. How a field goes together with its label, its description, and its messages is on the Forms page.

heading: Options
text: Every Radio inside the bar becomes an option. Its label is all that shows, so the description, the messages, and sitsOn on the radio itself are ignored inside a bar. Put error and hint on the bar instead.

heading: Surface
text: A bar works out what it is sitting on for itself, by asking the Card or Navbar it's inside. It takes the Input's edge rather than the Radio's, since the two sit side by side. The track is white on every surface, so the labels and the pill don't change with it. | Sitting on | Which is | Boundary | | ------------ | ------------ | ----------------- | | default | white | slate-200 border | | glass | slate-50 | slate-200 border | | sunken | slate-300/30 | shadow, no border | | dark | slate-700 | shadow, no border | | background | slate-200 | shadow, no border | Pass sitsOn on the page background, since nothing there can announce it. An element that paints a background of its own can wrap its contents in SurfaceProvider instead.

heading: Size
text: The size prop on the bar sets the track and every option in it. The sizes are sm, md (the default), and lg, at 32, 40, and 48px tall, which are the Input's sm, md, and lg. The labels run text-xs, text-sm, and text-base.

heading: Error and hint
text: error takes the message to show under the bar. It recolors the track's border, marks the line with a warning icon, sets aria-invalid on every option, and points each one's aria-describedby at the message. Pass an array for more than one message. hint is the same line before anything goes wrong, at slate-600 behind an info mark.

heading: Disabled
text: disabled on the bar fills the track slate-100 and drops the labels to slate-400. The picked option keeps its pill, with its label at slate-500, rather than losing the answer along with the control.

heading: Interaction
text: Hovering an unpicked option fills its pill slate-100 and lifts its label to slate-700. The picked option does nothing on hover, since there is nothing left for it to do. Picking an option slides the pill to it over 200ms, stretching or shrinking to the new label's width on the way. Pressing shrinks the label to 96% for the length of the press. The shrink is motion-safe, so it doesn't run for someone who has asked for reduced motion. Focus draws a blue outline around the option's cell, two pixels wide at a two pixel offset, and only for keyboard focus. Pressing it doesn't ring it. Everything else is the browser's. A bar is one tab stop, landing on whichever option is picked. The arrow keys move through the set and pick as they go, wrapping at either end.

The pill carries the answer, and at 1.2:1 against the white track it doesn't clear on its own. The picked label steps from slate-500 to slate-800 alongside it, so the weight of the text moves as well as the fill behind it. The disabled label runs slate-500 on slate-200 at 3.9:1. Disabled controls are exempt from the contrast rules, and it is deliberately quiet.

A switch is a that flips a boolean the moment it's pressed. It has two forms. The plain pill is a thumb sliding along a track. The labeled form puts the name of each state inside the track, and the thumb sits behind whichever one is current. Both are the same component, so the props, the states, and the keyboard behavior are the same. On the web, we almost always use the labeled version. The plain pill is reserved for the mobile app. A switch has no label of its own beside it. Give it a name with aria-label, or point aria-labelledby at the text next to it. The words inside the labeled form are hidden from assistive technology, since read together they'd name the control "Draft Live".

heading: Plain and labeled
text: Left alone, a switch is a pill. Pass on and off and it grows into the labeled form, with the text for each state inside the track. The on and off slots take the same place when the text needs markup. The two label columns are always the same width, taken from the longer of the two, so the thumb covers exactly half the track in either state. The inactive label drops to 40% opacity and the active one sits at full strength on the white thumb.

heading: Surface
text: A switch works out what it is sitting on for itself, by asking the Card or Navbar it's inside. The on track is sky-400 on every surface. The off track is slate-300, and steps away from the surface where slate-300 would vanish into it. On white it lightens to slate-200. On sunken it goes to slate-400 at 50%. On dark it goes the other way, to slate-800, so the switch reads as a well in the panel rather than a lighter patch on it. | Sitting on | Which is | Off track | | ------------ | ------------ | ------------- | | default | white | slate-200 | | glass | slate-50 | slate-300 | | sunken | slate-300/30 | slate-400/50 | | dark | slate-700 | slate-800 | | background | slate-200 | slate-300 | On dark the inactive label is white instead of slate-800 while the switch is off, since it sits on the slate-800 track. Once the switch is on, the track is sky-400 and the inactive label is slate-800 like everywhere else. The active label stays slate-800 on its white thumb. The track has a shallow inset shadow and a 1px bottom border in white, so it reads as pressed into the surface. The border is white at 80% on default, sunken, and background, solid white on glass, and white at 25% on dark. On a white card it vanishes into the card, which is fine, since the inset shadow still does the work. The page background is the surface nothing can announce. That's what sitsOn is for. An element that paints a background of its own can wrap its contents in SurfaceProvider instead.

heading: Size
text: The size prop sets the track, and in the labeled form the text and its padding too. The sizes are sm, md (the default), and lg. The pill is the height of a Checkbox box at each size. The labeled form is the height of a Button, so the two sit level in a toolbar. | Size | Pill | Labeled | | ---- | --------- | ------------------ | | sm | 16×28px | 32px, text-xs | | md | 20×36px | 40px, text-xs | | lg | 24×44px | 48px, text-sm |

heading: Loading
text: loading pulses the whole switch, swaps the cursor for a progress cursor, sets aria-busy, and ignores presses until it's cleared. The model isn't touched, so the switch holds the old state while the new one is on its way.

heading: Disabled
text: disabled flattens the track to slate-200 and the thumb to slate-50, and drops the labels to slate-400. On dark the track is slate-800 at 50%, the thumb slate-500, and the labels slate-300. The thumb keeps its position, so a disabled switch still shows which way it's set.

heading: Interaction
text: Hovering deepens the track, sky-400 to sky-500 at 80% when on, slate-200 to slate-300 when off on white, slate-300 to slate-400 at 60% when off on glass and background, slate-400 at 50% to solid slate-400 when off on sunken, and slate-800 to slate-900 when off on dark, and stretches the thumb to 105% of its width. Pressing stretches it to 110%. Both stretches are motion-safe, so they don't run for someone who has asked for reduced motion, and a disabled or loading switch doesn't stretch at all. The thumb takes 200ms to cross the track on an ease-out curve, quick and without a bounce, in line with Look and Feel. The label fades run 300ms. Focus draws a blue outline around the track, two pixels wide at a two pixel offset, and only for keyboard focus. Pressing the switch doesn't ring it. Everything else is the browser's. Tab reaches the switch, and Space and Enter both flip it, since it is a native button.
